title: Forces Acting on Structures and Mechanisms
unitGoal: Students will identify forces, loads, materials, shapes, and design choices that help structures and mechanisms work safely.

lessons.title: Structures and Forces
lessons.learningGoal: Students will identify structures, mechanisms, forces, and loads in everyday examples.
successCriteria: I can tell the difference between a structure and a mechanism.
I can identify pushes, pulls, and loads acting on objects.
I can explain how forces can change motion, shape, or stability.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise identifying structures, mechanisms, pushes, pulls, and loads.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that structures are built to support loads and mechanisms use moving parts to transfer force and motion.
lessons.christianFocus: Students can study design with gratitude for the order in God's created world and with care for the people who use structures and mechanisms.
lessonContent: A structure is something made of parts arranged to support a load or hold a shape.
A mechanism is a system with moving parts that transfers force or motion.
A force is a push or a pull.
Forces can change an object's motion, shape, or stability.
A load is a force carried by a structure, such as the weight of people, furniture, wind, snow, or the structure itself.

studentActivity.title: Structures and Forces Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise spotting structures, mechanisms, forces, and loads.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: built things have jobs
steps.text: A structure supports something or holds a shape. A mechanism has moving parts that transfer force or motion. Some objects, such as a bicycle, include both structures and mechanisms.

steps.title: Look for the Main Job
steps.prompt: Support or motion?
steps.text: To decide whether something is mainly a structure or mechanism, ask what its main job is. A bridge mainly supports loads. A door hinge mainly helps motion happen in a controlled way.

steps.title: Structure Example
steps.prompt: Which object is mainly a structure?
choices: a bridge deck that supports traffic
a gear train that turns another gear
a wheel and axle that helps a cart roll
steps.correctAnswer: a bridge deck that supports traffic
steps.feedback: Correct. A bridge deck is built to support loads.
steps.hint: Look for the choice whose main job is support.

steps.title: Mechanism Example
steps.prompt: Which object is mainly a mechanism?
choices: a bookshelf standing against a wall
steps.feedback: Yes. It has moving parts that transfer motion.
steps.hint: Mechanisms usually include moving parts.

steps.title: Both at Once
steps.prompt: Why can a bicycle be described as both a structure and a mechanism?
choices: Its frame supports the rider, and its moving parts transfer force and motion.
It is colourful, and colourful objects always have two science jobs.
It has wheels, so its frame no longer needs to support anything.
steps.correctAnswer: Its frame supports the rider, and its moving parts transfer force and motion.
steps.feedback: Correct. One object can include both support and motion systems.
steps.hint: Think about the frame and the moving parts.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A structure can be designed to hold a shape and support a load.
steps.feedback: Correct. Support and shape are key structure ideas.
steps.hint: A structure is not only a building.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised sorting structures and mechanisms.

steps.title: Forces Are Pushes and Pulls
steps.prompt: Loads are forces too
steps.text: A force is a push or pull. A load is a force a structure carries. A shelf carries the load of books, and a bridge carries loads from itself, traffic, wind, and weather.

steps.title: Push or Pull
steps.prompt: A student closes a drawer by pressing on it. What force is being used?
steps.feedback: Correct. Pressing the drawer inward is a push.
steps.hint: A push moves away from the person applying it.

steps.title: Load Example
steps.prompt: Which is a load on a classroom chair?
steps.feedback: Yes. The chair must support the student's weight.
steps.hint: A load is a force the structure carries.

steps.title: Force Effect
steps.prompt: A heavy backpack bends a hook slightly downward. What effect did the force have?
choices: It changed the hook's shape a little.
It turned the hook into a mechanism.
It removed all load from the hook.
steps.correctAnswer: It changed the hook's shape a little.
steps.feedback: Correct. Forces can change shape.
steps.hint: The hook bent under the load.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Wind can act as a load on a tall outdoor structure.
steps.feedback: Correct. Wind can push on a structure.
steps.hint: Loads are not only people or boxes.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised identifying forces and loads.

questions.prompt: What is a structure?
choices: parts arranged to support a load or hold a shape
any object that must include a battery
a material that cannot bend under any load
questions.correctAnswer: parts arranged to support a load or hold a shape
questions.reviewNote: Structures support loads or hold shapes.

questions.prompt: What is a mechanism?
choices: a system with moving parts that transfers force or motion
a structure that can never move
a load that is only caused by weather
questions.correctAnswer: a system with moving parts that transfers force or motion

questions.prompt: What is a force?
choices: only the weight of an object
questions.reviewNote: A force is a push or pull.

questions.prompt: Which is a load on a bridge?
choices: the name painted on a sign
questions.reviewNote: Traffic is a load the bridge carries.

questions.prompt: A shelf sags under heavy books. What has the load affected?
choices: the meaning of the word shelf
the fact that the books are books
questions.reviewNote: The shelf has bent under the load.

questions.prompt: Why can a bicycle include both a structure and mechanisms?
choices: The frame supports the rider, and the moving parts transfer motion.
The wheels are round, so the frame cannot support anything.
It has many parts, and every object with many parts is a mechanism only.
questions.correctAnswer: The frame supports the rider, and the moving parts transfer motion.
questions.reviewNote: A bicycle frame supports, while pedals, chain, and wheels move.

questions.prompt: A force can be a push or a pull.
Wind can be a load on an outdoor structure.

lessons.title: Compression, Tension, Torsion, and Shear
lessons.learningGoal: Students will identify four common types of forces and explain how they affect structures.
successCriteria: I can describe compression, tension, torsion, and shear.
I can match force types to everyday examples.
I can explain why knowing force types helps with safer design.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise identifying compression, tension, torsion, and shear in everyday examples.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that different forces affect structures in different ways and that designers must plan for those forces.
lessons.christianFocus: Students connect careful design with loving their neighbours by thinking about safety, reliability, and wise use of materials.
lessonContent: Compression is a squeezing or pressing force.
Tension is a stretching or pulling force.
Torsion is a twisting force.
Shear is a force that pushes parts of a material in opposite directions so they may slide or tear.
A structure may face more than one kind of force at the same time.

studentActivity.title: Force Types Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise naming force types in real examples.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: forces have different patterns
steps.text: Forces do not all act the same way. A force may squeeze, stretch, twist, or make parts slide past each other. Naming the force helps explain what is happening.

steps.title: Four Force Words
steps.prompt: Compression, tension, torsion, shear
steps.text: Compression squeezes. Tension stretches. Torsion twists. Shear pushes parts in opposite directions, like when scissors cut paper.

steps.title: Compression
steps.prompt: A stack of books presses down on a cardboard box. Which force is the box experiencing?
steps.feedback: Correct. The box is being squeezed by the load.
steps.hint: Compression presses or squeezes.

steps.title: Tension
steps.prompt: A rope is pulled tight during a tug-of-war. Which force is acting on the rope?
steps.feedback: Yes. Tension stretches or pulls a material.
steps.hint: Think about the rope being pulled.

steps.title: Torsion
steps.prompt: A screwdriver twists a screw into wood. Which force is being applied?
steps.feedback: Correct. Torsion is a twisting force.
steps.hint: Look for twisting.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Shear can happen when forces push parts of a material in opposite directions.
steps.feedback: Correct. Shear can cause sliding, tearing, or cutting.
steps.hint: Scissors cutting paper show shear.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised naming force types.

steps.title: Forces Affect Design
steps.prompt: Designers plan for force
steps.text: A safe structure needs to handle the forces it will face. Designers choose materials, shapes, and supports that resist compression, tension, torsion, and shear.

steps.title: Bridge Cable
steps.prompt: A bridge cable is pulled tight while supporting part of a bridge. Which force is most important in the cable?
steps.feedback: Correct. Cables often work well in tension.
steps.hint: Cables are pulled.

steps.title: Table Leg
steps.prompt: A table leg supports weight pressing downward from the tabletop. Which force is most likely acting on the leg?
steps.feedback: Yes. The leg is being squeezed by the load.
steps.hint: Table legs carry downward loads.

steps.title: Scissors
steps.prompt: Why do scissors show shear force?
choices: The blades push material in opposite directions to cut it.
The metal changes state when the blades touch.
steps.correctAnswer: The blades push material in opposite directions to cut it.
steps.feedback: Correct. Shear can cut or tear material.
steps.hint: Think about how the blades pass each other.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A real structure can experience more than one type of force at the same time.
steps.feedback: Correct. Structures often face several forces at once.
steps.hint: A bridge may face weight, wind, and movement.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised explaining force effects.

quiz.title: Compression, Tension, Torsion, and Shear Quiz

questions.prompt: Which force squeezes or presses a material?
Which force stretches or pulls a material?
Which force twists a material?
Which example best shows shear?
choices: a table leg being pressed downward
questions.reviewNote: Shear can cut or tear as parts move in opposite directions.

questions.prompt: A cable pulled tight on a bridge mainly experiences...
A column holding up a roof mainly experiences...
Designers should think about the forces a structure will face.
A structure can face compression and tension at the same time.
questions.reviewNote: Real structures often face several forces.

lessons.title: Loads and Stability
lessons.learningGoal: Students will explain how loads, centre of gravity, base size, and balance affect stability.
successCriteria: I can compare live loads, dead loads, and environmental loads.
I can explain how centre of gravity and base size affect stability.
I can choose design changes that improve stability.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise reasoning about loads, balance, centre of gravity, and stability.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that stable structures resist tipping, sliding, or collapsing under expected loads.
lessons.christianFocus: Students learn that safe design is one way people can serve and protect others.
lessonContent: A dead load is the weight of the structure itself.
A live load is the weight of things added to or moving on a structure, such as people, books, or vehicles.
Environmental loads include wind, rain, snow, ice, and earthquakes.
Stability means a structure resists tipping, sliding, or collapsing.
A lower centre of gravity and a wider base often make a structure more stable.

studentActivity.title: Stability Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise identifying loads and choosing ways to improve stability.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: structures carry different loads
steps.text: Structures must carry their own weight and other forces added to them. Designers think about expected loads before building.

steps.title: Three Load Types
steps.prompt: Dead, live, environmental
steps.text: Dead load is the structure's own weight. Live load is added weight such as people or vehicles. Environmental load comes from wind, snow, rain, ice, or ground movement.

steps.title: Dead Load
steps.prompt: Which is part of a bridge's dead load?
choices: the weight of the bridge materials
steps.correctAnswer: the weight of the bridge materials
steps.feedback: Correct. Dead load is the structure's own weight.
steps.hint: Dead load is built in.

steps.title: Live Load
steps.prompt: Which is a live load on a school floor?
choices: the weight of the floor itself
steps.feedback: Yes. People moving on a structure are live loads.
steps.hint: Live loads can change.

steps.title: Environmental Load
steps.prompt: Which is an environmental load on a roof?
choices: the wooden beams in the roof
a chair placed in the classroom
steps.feedback: Correct. Snow is an environmental load.
steps.hint: Weather can add loads.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A safe design should consider loads that may change over time.
steps.feedback: Correct. Live and environmental loads can change.
steps.hint: Think about people, weather, and use.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised identifying load types.

steps.title: What Makes Structures Stable?
steps.prompt: Balance matters
steps.text: A stable structure resists tipping, sliding, or collapsing. A wide base, lower centre of gravity, strong connections, and balanced loads can improve stability.

steps.title: Wider Base
steps.prompt: A tall tower model tips easily. Which change would likely improve stability?
steps.feedback: Correct. A wider base can improve stability.
steps.hint: A broad base helps resist tipping.

steps.title: Centre of Gravity
steps.prompt: Why can placing heavy parts lower make a structure more stable?
choices: It lowers the centre of gravity.
steps.correctAnswer: It lowers the centre of gravity.
steps.feedback: Yes. A lower centre of gravity often improves stability.
steps.hint: Think about balance.

steps.title: Balanced Load
steps.prompt: A shelf has all heavy books on one far end. What is a reasonable improvement?
choices: spread the load more evenly if the shelf is designed for it
add more heavy books to the same end
ignore it because loads cannot affect stability
steps.correctAnswer: spread the load more evenly if the shelf is designed for it
steps.feedback: Correct. Better load distribution can improve stability.
steps.hint: Uneven loads can matter.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A structure can be strong in one situation but unstable if the load changes.
steps.feedback: Correct. Load conditions affect stability.
steps.hint: A structure must match the load it faces.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised improving stability.

questions.prompt: What is a dead load?
choices: the weight of the structure itself
questions.correctAnswer: the weight of the structure itself

questions.prompt: Which is a live load on a bridge?
choices: the concrete in the bridge deck
snow resting on the bridge overnight

questions.prompt: Which is an environmental load?
What does stability mean?
choices: using only one type of material
questions.reviewNote: Stable structures resist unwanted movement or failure.

questions.prompt: Which change often makes a tower model more stable?
questions.reviewNote: A wider base can resist tipping.

questions.prompt: Why can a lower centre of gravity improve stability?
choices: The structure is less likely to tip.
The structure no longer has dead load.
The structure cannot be affected by wind.
questions.correctAnswer: The structure is less likely to tip.
questions.reviewNote: A lower centre of gravity helps with balance.

questions.prompt: Live loads can change while a structure is being used.
questions.reviewNote: People, vehicles, and movable objects can change.

questions.prompt: A safe design should consider likely loads before the structure is used.

lessons.title: Materials, Shapes, and Strength
lessons.learningGoal: Students will explain how materials, shapes, and bracing can make structures stronger or more stable.
successCriteria: I can compare materials by useful properties for structure design.
I can explain how shapes such as triangles, arches, and tubes can add strength.
I can choose design improvements using evidence from a test.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise connecting material properties, shapes, and bracing to structure strength.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that structures are not made stronger only by adding more material; shape and arrangement matter too.
lessons.christianFocus: Students consider wise stewardship by choosing materials thoughtfully instead of wasting them.
lessonContent: Materials have properties that affect how they perform in structures.
Strong structures often use shapes that spread forces well.
Triangles are often used because they resist changing shape.
Arches can spread loads outward and downward.
Tubes, folded shapes, and bracing can add strength without simply using much more material.
A good design uses evidence from testing to improve the structure.

studentActivity.title: Shape and Strength Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise choosing materials, shapes, and supports for stronger structures.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: material choices matter
steps.text: Different materials have different properties. A designer may think about strength, flexibility, mass, cost, water resistance, and how safely the material can be used.

steps.title: Strength Is Not the Only Property
steps.prompt: Choose for the job
steps.text: A material that is good for one structure may not be best for another. A bridge, umbrella, desk, and tent each need materials with different properties.

steps.title: Bridge Material
steps.prompt: A model bridge bends too much under a load. Which material property should the designer consider first?
choices: whether the material is the brightest colour
whether the material floats in a cup
steps.feedback: Correct. The bridge needs to resist bending under load.
steps.hint: Think about the problem shown in the test.

steps.title: Water Resistance
steps.prompt: A structure will be used outdoors in rain. Which property may matter?
steps.feedback: Yes. Rain can affect material choice.
steps.hint: Outdoor use adds weather concerns.

steps.title: Wise Use
steps.prompt: Why should a designer avoid using far more material than needed?
choices: It may waste resources without improving the design much.
More material always makes every structure safer.
Using extra material removes the need for testing.
steps.correctAnswer: It may waste resources without improving the design much.
steps.feedback: Correct. Wise design balances strength, safety, and resource use.
steps.hint: Stewardship means using resources carefully.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A material should be chosen based on the job the structure needs to do.
steps.feedback: Correct. Materials should fit the design problem.
steps.hint: Different jobs need different properties.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised choosing materials by properties.

steps.title: Shape Can Add Strength
steps.prompt: Arrangement matters
steps.text: A structure's shape can help it carry loads. Triangles often resist changing shape. Arches spread loads. Braces can stop parts from bending or leaning too far.

steps.title: Triangle Brace
steps.prompt: A rectangular frame wobbles side to side. Which change would likely help?
choices: add a diagonal brace to make triangles
paint the frame a darker colour
steps.correctAnswer: add a diagonal brace to make triangles
steps.feedback: Correct. Diagonal bracing can reduce wobbling.
steps.hint: Triangles resist changing shape.

steps.title: Arch
steps.prompt: Why can an arch be useful in a structure?
choices: It helps spread a load outward and downward.
It removes all forces from the structure.
It works only when no load is present.
steps.correctAnswer: It helps spread a load outward and downward.
steps.feedback: Yes. An arch spreads forces.
steps.hint: Think about how the load travels through the shape.

steps.title: Testing Evidence
steps.prompt: A student tests two paper beams. One folded beam holds more washers than a flat sheet. What does the evidence suggest?
choices: Folding changed the shape in a way that improved strength.
The washers became lighter during the second test.
Flat paper is not matter if it cannot hold a load.
steps.correctAnswer: Folding changed the shape in a way that improved strength.
steps.feedback: Correct. Shape can affect strength.
steps.hint: The material may be the same, but the shape changed.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Adding braces can help a structure resist bending or leaning.
steps.feedback: Correct. Bracing can strengthen a structure.
steps.hint: Braces support parts of a frame.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised using shapes and bracing to improve structures.

questions.prompt: Which property is important for a bridge material?
choices: whether it is stored near scissors

questions.prompt: Which property may matter for an outdoor structure?
questions.reviewNote: Rain and moisture can affect materials.

questions.prompt: Why should designers avoid wasting materials?
choices: Resources should be used wisely while still meeting safety needs.
Less planning always makes structures stronger.
Testing is unnecessary if extra material is added.
questions.correctAnswer: Resources should be used wisely while still meeting safety needs.
questions.reviewNote: Good design considers stewardship and safety.

questions.prompt: Why are triangles often used in structures?
choices: They turn every force into magnetism.
questions.reviewNote: Triangles are strong shapes for frames.

questions.prompt: How can an arch help a structure?
choices: It spreads a load outward and downward.
It makes the structure have no dead load.
It keeps all force in one tiny point.
questions.correctAnswer: It spreads a load outward and downward.

questions.prompt: A frame wobbles. Which change is most likely to help?
choices: place all weight on one side

questions.prompt: A change in shape can make the same material stronger in a structure.
The best material depends on the structure's purpose and conditions.
questions.reviewNote: Designers choose materials for the job.

lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise identifying mechanisms and explaining how they transfer force and motion.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that mechanisms use moving parts to make tasks easier, change direction, change speed, or transfer motion.

lessonContent: A mechanism has moving parts that transfer force or motion.
Levers, wheels and axles, gears, pulleys, hinges, and ramps are common mechanism examples.
A mechanism may change the direction of a force, change speed, or make a task easier.
Mechanisms need safe design because moving parts can pinch, slip, or break.
Useful technology should solve real problems without ignoring safety.

studentActivity.title: Mechanisms and Motion Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise explaining how mechanisms transfer force and motion.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: moving parts have jobs
steps.text: A mechanism uses moving parts to transfer force or motion. Mechanisms are found in scissors, bicycles, door hinges, can openers, clocks, and many machines.

steps.title: Simple Mechanisms
steps.prompt: Know common examples
steps.text: Levers, wheels and axles, gears, pulleys, hinges, and ramps can help people move loads, change direction, or make work easier.

steps.title: Lever
steps.prompt: Which object uses a lever?
choices: a seesaw lifting one side as the other side goes down
a plain brick wall holding its shape
a glass window that does not open
steps.correctAnswer: a seesaw lifting one side as the other side goes down
steps.feedback: Correct. A seesaw is a lever.
steps.hint: A lever pivots around a point.

steps.title: Wheel and Axle
steps.prompt: Which example uses a wheel and axle?
steps.feedback: Yes. A doorknob uses wheel-and-axle motion.
steps.hint: Look for round turning parts.

steps.title: Gears
steps.prompt: Why are gears useful in some mechanisms?
choices: They can transfer turning motion between parts.
They make a structure support loads without materials.
They dissolve when force is added.
steps.correctAnswer: They can transfer turning motion between parts.
steps.feedback: Correct. Gears transfer turning motion.
steps.hint: Gears have teeth that mesh.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A mechanism must have some part that moves.
steps.feedback: Correct. Mechanisms transfer force or motion through moving parts.
steps.hint: Moving parts are key.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised identifying mechanisms.

steps.title: Motion Can Change
steps.prompt: Direction, speed, or effort
steps.text: Mechanisms can change the direction of motion, transfer motion from one part to another, or make a task require less effort. Safe mechanisms also control motion so people are protected.

steps.title: Pulley
steps.prompt: How can a pulley help lift a flag?
choices: It changes the direction of the pulling force.
It makes the flag have no weight.
It changes the rope into a solid beam.
steps.correctAnswer: It changes the direction of the pulling force.
steps.feedback: Correct. Pulling down on the rope can lift the flag up.
steps.hint: Think about direction.

steps.title: Ramp
steps.prompt: Why can a ramp help move a load upward?
choices: It spreads the lifting over a longer distance.
It removes the force of gravity completely.
It turns the load into a gas.
steps.correctAnswer: It spreads the lifting over a longer distance.
steps.feedback: Yes. A ramp can reduce effort by increasing distance.
steps.hint: A ramp is an inclined plane.

steps.title: Safety
steps.prompt: Why should moving parts be designed carefully?
choices: They can pinch, slip, jam, or break if used poorly.
Fast-moving parts always make a mechanism safer.
steps.correctAnswer: They can pinch, slip, jam, or break if used poorly.
steps.feedback: Correct. Mechanism design must include safety.
steps.hint: Think about fingers, loads, and control.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A useful mechanism should solve a problem while still being safe to use.
steps.feedback: Correct. Usefulness and safety both matter.
steps.hint: Good design serves people.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised explaining mechanisms and motion.

questions.prompt: What does a mechanism do?
choices: transfers force or motion using moving parts
supports a load only by standing still
questions.correctAnswer: transfers force or motion using moving parts

questions.prompt: Which example is a lever?
questions.reviewNote: A seesaw pivots like a lever.

questions.prompt: Which object uses a wheel and axle?
questions.reviewNote: A doorknob turns around an axle.

questions.prompt: What can gears transfer?
How can a pulley help raise a flag?
choices: It changes the direction of the pulling force.
It removes all weight from the flag.
It makes the rope rigid like a beam.
questions.correctAnswer: It changes the direction of the pulling force.

questions.prompt: Why can a ramp help move something upward?
choices: It spreads the work over a longer distance.
It makes gravity stop acting on the load.
questions.correctAnswer: It spreads the work over a longer distance.
questions.reviewNote: A ramp can make lifting easier by increasing distance.

questions.prompt: Moving parts can create safety concerns if they pinch, jam, or break.
A mechanism can change the direction of a force.

I can use test evidence to improve a design.

lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that good design uses criteria, constraints, fair tests, evidence, and improvement.
lessons.christianFocus: Students practise perseverance, honesty, and stewardship as they improve designs and use materials wisely.
lessonContent: Design criteria tell what a design must do to be successful.
Constraints are limits such as time, materials, size, cost, or safety rules.
A prototype is a test version of a design.
A fair test changes one important thing at a time when possible and measures results carefully.
A good redesign is based on evidence, not just guessing or copying.

studentActivity.title: Design and Test Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise planning fair structure tests and improving designs with evidence.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: design has a goal
steps.text: A design problem needs clear criteria and constraints. Criteria tell what success means. Constraints tell the limits you must work within.

steps.title: Prototype First
steps.prompt: Test versions help learning
steps.text: A prototype is a test version. It may not work perfectly at first. Testing helps a designer learn what to improve.

steps.title: Criteria
steps.prompt: A class must build a paper bridge that holds at least 20 washers. What is the design criterion?
choices: It must hold at least 20 washers.
It must be made during science class.
It must use only the paper provided.
steps.correctAnswer: It must hold at least 20 washers.
steps.feedback: Correct. Criteria tell what success means.
steps.hint: Look for the goal the design must meet.

steps.title: Constraint
steps.prompt: A group may use only 2 sheets of paper and 30 cm of tape. What is this?
steps.feedback: Yes. Material limits are constraints.
steps.hint: Constraints are limits.

steps.title: Prototype
steps.prompt: Why build a prototype?
choices: to test and improve a design before treating it as finished
to prove the first idea is always best
steps.correctAnswer: to test and improve a design before treating it as finished
steps.feedback: Correct. Prototypes help designers learn.
steps.hint: A prototype is a test version.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A design can have both criteria and constraints.
steps.feedback: Correct. Designs have goals and limits.
steps.hint: Most real design problems have both.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised planning a design.

steps.title: Evidence Guides Redesign
steps.prompt: Measure before changing
steps.text: A fair test uses careful measurements and clear conditions. If a bridge fails, the designer should notice where and how it failed before making changes.

steps.title: Fair Test
steps.prompt: Two bridge designs are tested. Which setup is fairest?
choices: Use the same supports and add washers one at a time in the same place.
Use different supports and different loads for each bridge.
Stop testing the second bridge when it looks weaker.
steps.correctAnswer: Use the same supports and add washers one at a time in the same place.
steps.feedback: Correct. Fair tests keep important conditions the same.
steps.hint: Compare one design difference at a time when possible.

steps.title: Useful Evidence
steps.prompt: A bridge bends in the middle after 12 washers. Which note is most useful for redesign?
choices: The middle span needs better support or shape.
The bridge did not like the washers.
The group should choose the answer before testing.
steps.correctAnswer: The middle span needs better support or shape.
steps.feedback: Yes. It uses evidence from where the bridge failed.
steps.hint: Look for the evidence-based improvement.

steps.title: Redesign
steps.prompt: Which redesign choice is most responsible?
choices: Improve one part based on test evidence and retest.
Add random materials until the bridge looks larger.
Ignore the failed test and submit the same prototype.
steps.correctAnswer: Improve one part based on test evidence and retest.
steps.feedback: Correct. Redesign should use evidence.
steps.hint: Good improvement is not random.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A design that fails a test can still teach useful information.
steps.feedback: Correct. Testing helps reveal what to improve.
steps.hint: A failed test is evidence, not wasted learning.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised testing and improving a structure.

quiz.title: Designing and Testing a Structure Quiz

questions.prompt: What are design criteria?
choices: the features a design must have to be successful
the weather around an outdoor structure
the total weight of a finished bridge only
questions.correctAnswer: the features a design must have to be successful

questions.prompt: What are constraints?
choices: limits such as materials, time, size, cost, or safety rules
extra loads added after testing only
questions.correctAnswer: limits such as materials, time, size, cost, or safety rules

questions.prompt: What is a prototype?
choices: a test version of a design
a final answer that cannot change
a material with no measurable properties
questions.correctAnswer: a test version of a design
questions.reviewNote: A prototype is built to test and learn.

questions.prompt: Which testing setup is fairest?
choices: same supports and same way of adding load for each bridge
different supports and different load positions for each bridge
testing only the design that looks strongest
questions.correctAnswer: same supports and same way of adding load for each bridge

questions.prompt: What should guide a redesign?
A tower tips when weight is added high up. Which improvement fits the evidence?
choices: lower the heavy part or widen the base
questions.correctAnswer: lower the heavy part or widen the base

questions.prompt: A design problem can include both criteria and constraints.
questions.reviewNote: Designs usually have goals and limits.

questions.prompt: A failed prototype can provide useful evidence for improvement.
questions.reviewNote: Failures can show what needs redesign.

lessons.title: Real-World Structures and Safety
lessons.learningGoal: Students will connect structure and mechanism ideas to real-world safety, maintenance, and responsible design.
successCriteria: I can identify forces and loads in real-world structures.
I can explain why inspection and maintenance matter.
I can choose responsible design decisions that consider safety and use.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise applying structure and mechanism ideas to bridges, towers, buildings, playground equipment, and safety decisions.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students learn that real-world structures must be designed, inspected, maintained, and used responsibly.
lessons.christianFocus: Students connect safety and maintenance with loving their neighbours and caring for the built world responsibly.
lessonContent: Real-world structures and mechanisms are designed for users and conditions.
Designers must consider loads, forces, materials, shapes, weather, and how people will use the object.
Inspection means checking for damage, wear, weakness, or unsafe conditions.
Maintenance means caring for and repairing a structure or mechanism so it keeps working safely.
Responsible design thinks about safety, usefulness, cost, materials, and care for people.
practiceIdeas: Share the student mission for practice stars.
Use the lesson quiz as the scored check.
Review missed ideas before assigning the next Forces Acting on Structures and Mechanisms lesson.

studentActivityPlan.title: Real-World Safety Mission
studentActivityPlan.description: Practise applying forces, structures, mechanisms, and safety ideas to real examples.
studentActivityPlan.reward: 10 practice stars after each completed level

quizPlan.title: Real-World Structures and Safety Quiz
quizPlan.format: Multiple choice and true/false questions with one score at the end.
quizPlan.focus: Real-world forces, loads, inspection, maintenance, safety, users, and responsible design

lessons.assessmentPlan: Use the activity to build confidence and the quiz to check independent understanding.

studentActivity.title: Real-World Safety Mission
studentActivity.mission: Practise applying forces, structures, mechanisms, and safety ideas to real examples.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: real structures face real conditions
steps.text: Bridges, towers, shelves, playground equipment, bicycles, and buildings all face forces. Designers must think about how each structure or mechanism will actually be used.

steps.title: Users and Conditions
steps.prompt: Design for real life
steps.text: A real design should consider users, loads, weather, materials, motion, and safety. A structure that works indoors may need changes before it is safe outdoors.

steps.title: Bridge Use
steps.prompt: Why must a pedestrian bridge be designed for more than its own weight?
choices: It must also support people, weather loads, and movement.
Its colour controls how much force exists.
A bridge's own weight is never a load.
steps.correctAnswer: It must also support people, weather loads, and movement.
steps.feedback: Correct. Real bridges face several loads.
steps.hint: Think about dead, live, and environmental loads.

steps.title: Playground Equipment
steps.prompt: Which question is most important for playground safety?
choices: Can it support expected users and remain stable during use?
Does it look like the tallest structure nearby?
Can every moving part be hidden from view?
steps.correctAnswer: Can it support expected users and remain stable during use?
steps.feedback: Yes. Safety depends on loads, stability, and proper use.
steps.hint: Think about the children who use it.

steps.title: Outdoor Conditions
steps.prompt: A structure is moved from a dry classroom to an outdoor garden. What new condition may matter?
choices: rain, wind, sun, and changing temperature
whether the structure has a title
whether it was tested by only one student
steps.correctAnswer: rain, wind, sun, and changing temperature
steps.feedback: Correct. Outdoor conditions can affect design.
steps.hint: Weather creates new loads and material concerns.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A real-world structure should be designed for the way people will actually use it.
steps.feedback: Correct. User needs and real conditions matter.
steps.hint: Design is for real use, not just appearance.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised noticing real-world design clues.

steps.title: Structures Need Care
steps.prompt: Safe today and later
steps.text: Even a well-designed structure can wear out or become damaged. Inspection and maintenance help people notice problems before they become dangerous.

steps.title: Inspection
steps.prompt: What is the purpose of inspecting a structure?
choices: to look for damage, wear, weakness, or unsafe conditions
to prove no structure can ever fail
to replace design criteria with opinions
steps.correctAnswer: to look for damage, wear, weakness, or unsafe conditions
steps.feedback: Correct. Inspection checks for possible problems.
steps.hint: Inspection means careful checking.

steps.title: Maintenance
steps.prompt: Why does maintenance matter?
choices: It helps a structure or mechanism keep working safely over time.
It makes all loads disappear from the structure.
It means no testing was ever needed.
steps.correctAnswer: It helps a structure or mechanism keep working safely over time.
steps.feedback: Yes. Maintenance supports safety and function.
steps.hint: Think about repairs and care.

steps.title: Responsible Design
steps.prompt: Which design choice best shows care for users?
choices: include safety, expected loads, and clear use instructions
focus only on appearance and ignore load tests
make moving parts faster without checking pinch points
steps.correctAnswer: include safety, expected loads, and clear use instructions
steps.feedback: Correct. Responsible design protects users.
steps.hint: Safety is part of serving people well.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A structure that was safe when new may still need inspection later.
steps.feedback: Correct. Wear, damage, and changing conditions can matter.
steps.hint: Safe design includes care over time.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised applying safety and maintenance ideas.

questions.prompt: Why must a bridge be designed for more than its own weight?
choices: It may carry people, vehicles, wind, snow, and movement.
Its colour changes all loads into dead loads.
Its own weight is never part of design.
questions.correctAnswer: It may carry people, vehicles, wind, snow, and movement.
questions.reviewNote: Bridges face dead, live, and environmental loads.

questions.prompt: Which outdoor condition can affect a structure?
choices: the number of words in its name
whether it has been drawn in a notebook

questions.prompt: Which question matters most for playground equipment?
choices: Is it stable and strong enough for expected users?
Is it the brightest object outside?
Can it avoid all inspection forever?
questions.correctAnswer: Is it stable and strong enough for expected users?

questions.prompt: What does inspection mean?
choices: checking for damage, wear, weakness, or unsafe conditions
using a structure without looking at it
questions.correctAnswer: checking for damage, wear, weakness, or unsafe conditions

questions.prompt: Why is maintenance important?
choices: It helps structures and mechanisms keep working safely.
It means forces no longer act on structures.
It replaces the need for responsible use.
questions.correctAnswer: It helps structures and mechanisms keep working safely.

questions.prompt: Which design choice best shows care for users?
choices: testing expected loads and giving clear use instructions
hiding weak parts because they look untidy
choosing only the cheapest material without testing
questions.correctAnswer: testing expected loads and giving clear use instructions

questions.prompt: Real structures should be designed for the conditions they will face.
A safe structure may still need inspection as it gets older.
questions.reviewNote: Structures can wear or become damaged.

quiz.title: Forces Acting on Structures and Mechanisms Unit Quiz

questions.prompt: What is a structure?
choices: parts arranged to support a load or hold a shape
any object that must have a motor
a moving part with no load
questions.correctAnswer: parts arranged to support a load or hold a shape
questions.reviewNote: Structures support loads or hold shape.

questions.prompt: What is a mechanism?
choices: a system with moving parts that transfers force or motion
a solid material that can never move
a weather load on a bridge
questions.correctAnswer: a system with moving parts that transfers force or motion

questions.prompt: What is a force?
choices: only the colour of a material
only the height of a structure
questions.reviewNote: A force is a push or pull.

questions.prompt: Which force squeezes a material?
Which force stretches or pulls a material?
Which example shows torsion?
choices: twisting a screw with a screwdriver
questions.correctAnswer: twisting a screw with a screwdriver

questions.prompt: Which example shows shear?
questions.reviewNote: Shear can happen when parts are pushed in opposite directions.

questions.prompt: What is a dead load?
choices: the weight of the structure itself
a person walking across a floor
questions.correctAnswer: the weight of the structure itself

questions.prompt: Which is a live load?
choices: the wood in the chair frame
questions.reviewNote: People using a structure are live loads.

questions.prompt: Which is an environmental load?
choices: a backpack placed on a desk

questions.prompt: Which change often improves a tower's stability?
questions.reviewNote: A wider base can resist tipping.

questions.prompt: Why can heavy parts lower down improve stability?
choices: They lower the centre of gravity.
questions.correctAnswer: They lower the centre of gravity.
questions.reviewNote: A lower centre of gravity can reduce tipping.

questions.prompt: Which property matters for a structure used outdoors?
choices: whether it has the nicest name
whether it can be tasted safely
questions.reviewNote: Outdoor structures may face rain or moisture.

questions.prompt: Why are triangles often used in frames?
choices: They remove the need for connections.

questions.prompt: A rectangular frame wobbles. What is a likely improvement?
choices: place every load on one side

questions.prompt: How can a pulley help lift a flag?
choices: It changes the direction of the pulling force.
It changes the rope into a beam.
questions.correctAnswer: It changes the direction of the pulling force.

questions.prompt: What can gears transfer?
Which bridge test is fairest?
choices: same supports and same method for adding load
different supports and different loads each time
testing only the bridge that looks strongest
questions.correctAnswer: same supports and same method for adding load

questions.prompt: What should guide a redesign?
Why are inspection and maintenance important?
choices: They help structures and mechanisms stay safe over time.
They mean testing was never needed.
questions.correctAnswer: They help structures and mechanisms stay safe over time.
questions.reviewNote: Structures need care after they are built.
